xref.title: The Skatalites (Jamaica, 1963–1967) – Trombone-Led Studio Band; Played on Virtually Every Jamaican Record; Don Drummond Murdered His Girlfriend; Died in Asylum 1969
xref.body: Don Drummond was a trombone player who gave Jamaican ska a slightly darker feel. He first called his group The Satellites, then changed the name to The Skatalites. The Skatalites played on virtually every record made in Jamaica between 1963 and 1967, functioning as the equivalent of the studio bands at Motown and Stax in America. Their choppy sound became hugely influential and may have given ska its name. Unfortunately, Don Drummond never saw what became of his invention — in 1964 he murdered his girlfriend and died in an insane asylum in 1969, some say of natural causes, others say he was murdered by gangsters avenging his girlfriend's death, and some claim it was a government plot to suppress the powerful Jamaican music scene. "The SCA-TILites played on virtually every record made in Jamaica between 1963 and 1967."

xref.title: "Man Dress" Controversy (November 1970 - June 1971)
xref.body: David Bowie's decision to wear a full-length blue dress on the original cover of *The Man Who Sold the World* album in November 1970 was a highly controversial move in America. At the time, Bowie had little reputation in the US, and the country was not "ready for a feminized rocker." This led to record stores refusing to stock the album until RCA Records provided an alternative cover, and even an incident where a gun was pulled on Bowie in Texas. "America, not ready for a guy wearing a dress."

xref.title: Elton John Gorilla Suit Incident – Richards, Atlanta, October 1973
xref.body: In October 1973, Iggy Pop and the Stooges were playing at Richards in Atlanta at the same time Elton John was touring America. Elton — engaged in a semi-friendly rivalry with David Bowie, who was a known Stooges supporter — decided to crash the show dressed in a full gorilla suit to surprise Iggy on stage. A photographer from Detroit music magazine *Creem* was tipped off. No one warned Iggy that this was planned, and no one warned Elton that Iggy was heavily intoxicated on speed that night. When Elton bounded onto the stage in the gorilla suit, Iggy genuinely believed it was a real gorilla, was terrified, and fled the stage. The incident was captured on film. After Elton removed the gorilla head and multiple people calmed Iggy down, the show resumed and the two performed several songs together — Iggy bare-chested, Elton still in the suit. "Iggy thought it was an actual gorilla. And this freak out is captured on film."

xref.title: Cocaine Addiction and Paranoia in Los Angeles (1974-1976)
xref.body: Between 1974 and 1976, Bowie was deeply entrenched in cocaine and alcohol addiction, a state exacerbated by his move to Los Angeles, the "cocaine capital of North America." This led to severe cocaine-induced paranoia, a common reaction among users, with Bowie's focus on witches. "Between 1974 and sometime in 1976, Bowie was an absolute mess."

xref.title: Cleveland Origin and Sound (1975)
xref.body: Pere Ubu emerged from Cleveland, having reorganized from the band Rocket from the Tombs in 1975. They were part of a scene of "extreme groups" that were artsy, anti-hippie, anti-establishment, and experimental. They began releasing self-produced indie singles in 1975. "Eventually we organized itself as Pair Ubu. In 1975, they began to release a series of self-produced indie singles that reached a few selecteers around North America. And even as far away as the UK."

xref.title: Conquest of England (July 4 & 6, 1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played two pivotal shows in London, first at the Roundhouse (capacity 2,000) on America's bicentennial, and then at Dingwalls two nights later. Despite their European record company trying to cancel gigs, the band delivered explosive performances. These concerts were England's "first proper exposure" to US-style punk rock and are credited with transforming nearly every major player in the burgeoning British punk rock scene, including members of the Sex Pistols, The Clash, The Pretenders, The Damned, and Generation X. "And over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th, 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

xref.title: Inspiration for British Punk (1976)
xref.body: The Ramones played a pivotal gig at the Roundhouse in London on Sunday, July 4th, 1976, as part of America's Bicentennial. Around 2,000 members of the "infant UK punk community" packed the venue, eager to hear the New York sound. This performance, along with another at Dingwalls, was immensely influential; key figures like Johnny Rotten and Joe Strummer attended soundchecks and shows, stating that the Ramones "turned them on" and "inspired them to form their own bands." The band felt like "royalty" upon arrival, noting the shift from selling out CBGB's to playing for 3,000 kids already "tuned in." "No one could have known it at the time, but this was one of the most influential gigs in the history of rock."

xref.title: First American Band to Tour Soviet Union (1977)
xref.body: In 1977, the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band was chosen over more conventional acts like the Doobie Brothers and America to be the first American band to tour the Soviet Union. This tour, endorsed by President Jimmy Carter, aimed to undermine communism through rock and roll. The tour proved immensely successful among young people in Russia and other Soviet republics, generating such high demand for tickets that it overwhelmed the KGB. "To be the first American band to tour through the Soviet Union, President Jimmy Carter was all for this, thinking that rock and roll could undermine communism."

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour – January 1978
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren's plan to "conquer America" with the Sex Pistols resulted in one of rock history's most disastrous road trips. Initially, the group's visa applications were denied, forcing them to cancel an important appearance on Saturday Night Live, where Elvis Costello was called in as a last-minute replacement. The drummer for Elvis Costello's performance notably wore a t-shirt that read "Thanks, milk," a sarcastic jab at Malcolm McLaren. McLaren made a bizarre miscalculation about American culture by routing the tour away from major cities and through the deep South, an area not receptive to punk rock values. "Instead, what he got was one of the most disastrous road trips in the history of rock."

xref.title: Columbus Holiday Inn Bar Fight (March 10, 1979) – Racist Remarks, Punch from Bonnie Bramlett, Career Nearly Ruined in America
xref.body: On March 10, 1979, Elvis Costello and his entourage were drinking heavily in a bar at a Holiday Inn in Columbus, Ohio, when they encountered Stephen Stills's party. Costello made blatant racist remarks about Ray Charles and James Brown. Stephen Stills's companion Bonnie Bramlett punched Costello, a full brawl broke out, and the incident made national news. American media sided with Stills; Costello became toxic and his American career took years to recover. He later described the incident in his memoirs *Unfaithful Music and Disappearing Ink* (2015) and acknowledged it without denial or excuse. "An old barfight from 37 years ago — but there are real serious things that haven't been fixed that are not my doing or my responsibility."

xref.title: Suicide (May 18, 1980)
xref.body: After previous suicide attempts, Ian Curtis took his own life by hanging himself from a clothesline in his kitchen in the early morning hours of May 18, 1980. This tragic event occurred on the very day Joy Division was scheduled to depart for their first-ever tour of North America. "There had been some suicide attempts. By the early morning hours of May 18, 1980, Ian couldn't take it anymore. He hanged himself from the clothesline in the kitchen of his house. That Monday was the day joy division was supposed to leave for their first ever tour of North America."

xref.title: Indie Roots and Mainstream Growth (1982-1985)
xref.body: R.E.M. started as a no-name indie band from the Deep South, releasing their first records on Hib-Tone before moving to IRS Records, an indie label run by Miles Copeland. Between 1982 and 1985, they released five albums on IRS, earning respect as pioneers of the college rock scene in North America, while also gaining a mainstream following due to their accessible music. xref.title: Mother's Murder (March 3, 1983) – Boyfriend John "Dean" Ricardi Shot Connie and Friend, Caught via America's Most Wanted
xref.body: Dave Navarro was 15 years old when his mother Connie — one of the models on *Let's Make a Deal* with Monty Hall — was shot to death along with her best friend Sue by her ex-boyfriend, a bodybuilder named John Ricardi (who went by "Dean"). After the relationship deteriorated and Connie sought a restraining order, Ricardi broke into the house on the night of March 3, 1983, and waited. Dave narrowly escaped by spending the weekend with his father. Ricardi evaded capture for almost eight years until a tip from a viewer of *America's Most Wanted* led to his arrest in Houston, Texas, on January 4, 1991. Dave testified against him at trial; Ricardi was subsequently placed on death row at San Quentin. "Human beings are not equipped to know how to handle something like that."

xref.title: Discovery of Death (2015)
xref.body: On December 2nd, 2015, Scott Weiland went for drinks with his bassist before returning to the bus, which then traveled to Minnesota. Around 9 AM on December 3rd, he used the bathroom and returned to bed. Later that day, the bus parked at a Country Inn and Suites in Bloomington, Minnesota, near Minneapolis, ahead of a show at the Medina Entertainment Center. Scott remained in his room. The band went for breakfast and later to the Mall of America, leaving Scott alone, as was often the case. His wife Jamie received a text from him but couldn't reach him by text or phone later. At 7 PM, she called the band's tour manager, ex-Marine Aaron Moller, who, just after 8 PM, found Scott lying in a fetal position in his room, eyes half-closed, with his body already stiff. "At around 9 in the morning of the third, Scott got up to use the bathroom and then went back to bed."

xref.title: Final Tour and Discovery (November - December 3, 2015)
xref.body: In November 2015, Scott Weiland embarked on a solo tour with his wife Jamie. Despite promising to get sober upon returning home, he was drinking heavily. They were last together on American Thanksgiving. On December 2, he went out for drinks with his bassist before returning to the tour bus, which then traveled to Minnesota. On December 3, the bus stopped in Bloomington, Minnesota, ahead of a show at the Medina Entertainment Center. Weiland remained asleep in his room at the back of the bus while the band went for breakfast and later to the Mall of America, which was a common occurrence. At 7 PM, his wife Jamie, unable to reach him via text or phone, called the tour manager, Aaron Moller. At around 8 PM, Moller found Weiland in his room, lying in a fetal position with half-closed eyes, his body already stiff. A 911 call was made at 8:22 PM, and paramedics declared him dead by 8:45 PM. xref.title: "Vs." Anti-System Release Strategy
xref.body: Pearl Jam deliberately released *Vs.* in stages, with the vinyl edition first appearing in the UK on October 11, 1993, followed by North America on October 12. The CD and cassette versions were delayed until October 18 and 19, respectively. This staggered release was a conscious effort by the band to "mess with the system" and "stick it to the label," Epic Records, which they felt was trying to kill off vinyl in favor of more expensive and profitable CDs. In 1993, none of the band members even owned a CD player, and Jeff Ament preferred a cassette version as his primary listening format. Further challenging the label, the vinyl edition was released without the album title or band name printed on it, forcing Epic to add a sticker to the shrink wrap. "Why? Phil Jim just wanted to mess with the system. So they did. In their mind, it was another way to stick it to the label."

xref.body: The name 54-40 came from Brad Merritt's stream-of-consciousness naming session in which he generated ideas including "Bridge View Dogs" (after their Surrey rehearsal space area) and "Safeway Rebels." He landed on 54-40, the slogan of US presidential candidate James Polk, who in the 1840s argued that America should take the entire Oregon Territory up to latitude 54°40' North — which included what is now British Columbia, at the time shared with Britain. The two founders had both moved around extensively (Merritt in the US, Osborne across Canada) and had met in high school in Tsawwassen, literally on the US border. "I wanted something which was big and yet small at the same time."

xref.body: The exemption of thousands of young British men from military service following the end of national service in 1957 and 1960 created ample free time. The Beatles, after a few years, broke through, igniting the British music scene and subsequently leading the British Invasion of North America. "After a couple of years, the Beatles broke through. xref.body: The English Beat were among the "unknown English bands" that legendary record executive Seymour Stein, founder of Sire Records, imported into North America, contributing to their rise in popularity. "He's the guy that imported unknown English bands like The Smiths and The Pretenders and The English Beat into North America."

xref.title: North American Non-Mainstream Rock (Late 1980s)
xref.body: At the end of the 1980s, R.E.M. represented the kind of non-mainstream rock that fans in North America were listening to, often found in small clubs or independent record stores. This taste was in opposition to mainstream genres like hair metal or Top 40 radio. "If you're in North America and into non-mainstream rock, you're into bands like REM and Sonic Youth and Hardcore Punk and the cooler Technopop bands from the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: North American Non-Mainstream Rock (Late 1980s)
xref.body: In the late 1980s, Sonic Youth was a prominent example of the non-mainstream rock and hardcore punk preferred by fans in North America who sought music beyond the mainstream. This audience typically frequented small, dark clubs and independent record stores. "If you're in North America and into non-mainstream rock, you're into bands like REM and Sonic Youth and Hardcore Punk and the cooler Technopop bands from the UK."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: North American Success and John Hughes (1980s)
xref.body: After signing with A&M Records, OMD gained significant traction in North America, particularly Canada. Their profile was further boosted when filmmaker John Hughes began featuring their music in his films, first with "Tesla Girls" in "Weird Science," and then by commissioning a song for "Pretty in Pink." "We moved to A&M and that's when they started to push us. And then two years into our A&M career, yeah, John Hughes came along."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Golden Age of Synths as told by OMD

xref.title: Oasis Reunion and World Tour Planned (Future)
xref.body: Oasis is planning a reunion and a world tour scheduled for the "next summer." Confirmed shows include locations in the UK and Ireland, Toronto (at Dan's View Park in August), several cities in the US, Mexico City, Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and South America. "Oasis is back together in touring next summer. So far, we know of shows in the UK and Ireland to hear in Toronto with Dan's View Park in August, and then onto the US for a few cities as well as Mexico City. And then there's Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and South America."

xref.title: Outrageous Behavior
xref.body: Iggy Pop was known for his "outrageous behavior" and "extreme things" performed with his band The Stooges in America, which directly influenced David Bowie's creation of the Ziggy Stardust character. "Iggy Pop, who was doing all kinds of extreme things in America with his band, The Stooges."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The Surprising History of Glam Rock

xref.title: Owner of Torpedo Comics
xref.body: John Dolmayan, the drummer for System of a Down, is also the proprietor of Torpedo Comics, recognized as one of America's premier comic book stores. Located in Las Vegas, the store operates out of a 3,500 square foot space and has been in business since 2003, specializing in rare comic books. "He's also the owner of one of the best comic book stores in America. It's called Turpedo Comics."

xref.title: Parallel Ascent with Indie Music
xref.body: R.E.M.'s evolution from a "fratboy band" to intelligent, articulate, and politically aware superstars mirrored the rise of indie music in America. For many, R.E.M. served as an entry point into a rock and roll universe that had remained largely undetected by the mainstream for over a decade, and their popularity growth was a testament to the power of college radio. "REM's rise from fratboy band to intelligent, articulate, and politically aware superstars paralleled the ascent of indie music in America."

xref.title: Personal Tragedies and Temporary Retirement from Rush
xref.body: The late 1990s were an exceptionally difficult period for Neil Peart, leading to a temporary retirement from Rush. On August 10, 1997, his 19-year-old daughter, Selina, died in a single-car accident while driving to university. Just five months later, his common-law wife of 23 years, Jackie, passed away from cancer. This double trauma prompted him to temporarily step away from the band to cope, embarking on a motorcycle tour across North America to help process his grief. "An August 10th, 1997, Neil's 19 year old daughter, Selina, died in a single car accident."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Peruvian Singer Ramillo Sevedra Alive Theory
xref.body: A conspiracy theory emerged from Peru when a singer named Ramillo Sevedra, who looked strikingly similar to Kurt Cobain, performed "Come As You Are" on a local TV station, with footage going viral. The accompanying story suggested Kurt was hiding in South America. However, this theory is debunked by the fact that Sevedra plays guitar right-handed, whereas Cobain was left-handed. "Someone noticed that a singer named Ramillo Sevedra looks a lot like Kurt."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Post-Bauhaus Success
xref.body: Formed by Daniel Ash, David J, and Kevin Haskins after Peter Murphy declined a Bauhaus reunion, Love and Rockets achieved greater commercial success than Bauhaus. They sold millions of records worldwide, headlined large tours, and secured a Top 40 hit in America. "Daniel Ash, David J and Kevin Haskins were far more successful than Bajaos could have ever been selling millions of records around the world, playing huge headline tours, and even having a top 40 hit in America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: What's The Big Deal About Bauhaus?

xref.title: Post-Breakup Activities of Members – Jones, Cook, Rotten
xref.body: After the breakup, guitarist Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook went to South America and recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten (John Liden) traveled to Jamaica to relax, immerse himself in reggae music, and smoke ganja. "Guitar Steve Jones and drummer Paul Cook ended up in South America where they recorded with an exiled British criminal. Johnny Rotten eventually turned up in Jamaica to decompress, soak up some reggae and smoke some ganja."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pre-Punk Pioneers
xref.body: Retroactively, Death, composed of three black men from Detroit, is now considered one of the most important pre-punk bands in America, having been significantly overlooked in their original era. "three black men from Detroit, who, albeit retroactively, are considered to be one of the most important pre-punk bands in America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Privacy in America
xref.body: Frischmann enjoyed living in the United States because no one recognized her, offering a stark contrast to the UK where her personal life was often scrutinized. She decided to stay in America for this reason. "No one knew who she was and unlike the UK, there wasn't someone always around digging into her personal life."

xref.title: Pushing Musical Boundaries
xref.body: As the 1980s progressed, Sonic Youth's music became more structured, but they consistently pushed the edge of the musical envelope. A deal with Black Flag's indie label, SST Records, helped them spread their influence throughout North America. "Although Sonic Youth's music became more structured as the 80s progressed, there was always the sense that they were pushing the edge of the musical envelope and thanks to a deal with black flags, indie label, SST records, they were able to spread their influence throughout North America."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

xref.title: Radio Ban in North America
xref.body: In North America, punk music, including The Ramones, faced significant resistance from radio stations due to its perceived political, class-oriented, crass, vulgar, and violent nature. "Radio stations wouldn't touch the Ramones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Record Label Hesitation in America
xref.body: The Clash's record label was hesitant to release their records in America, reflecting the general difficulty punk music faced in gaining traction in North America due to its controversial image. "The clash's record label was afraid to put our clash records in America."

xref.title: Rio PMP-300 Launch Support
xref.body: As the best-known performer among those who supported the launch of the Diamond Rio PMP-300, Frank Black and the Catholics contributed a song to the 100 tracks bundled for Rio customers. "Frank Black and the Catholics, a song that helped launch the Rio PMP-300, the first portable MP3 player to go on sale in North America."

xref.title: Rise via College Radio
xref.body: R.E.M.'s rootsy, made-in-America, anti-synthesizer guitar pop initially stood out from the dominant British new wave of the early 1980s and became a staple on college radio across North America. As their popularity grew, commercial radio stations began to follow suit, leading to album sales escalating from the tens of thousands to hundreds of thousands, and eventually into the millions. "REM became a staple of college radio across North America, and as the band's popularity grew, more commercial radio stations began to catch on."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: The History of Indie Rock: Part 3

xref.title: Self-Financed Self-Promoter
xref.body: Grant McDonald, based in Toronto, is noted for being entirely self-financed and an "incredible self-promoter," actively distributing his material and various memorabilia to radio stations across North America. He operates independently in his artistic and activist pursuits. "Other than the fact that he's from Toronto, and that he seems to be completely self-financed and is an incredible self-promoter."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Death and Ashes Disposition
xref.body: Sid Vicious died of a heroin overdose in his sleep in the early morning hours of February 2nd, 1979, at 63 Bank Street in Greenwich Village, New York, while out on bail awaiting trial for the death of Nancy Spungen. He was cremated because no funeral home would take his business. A legend, though unproven, suggests he died with a note asking to be buried next to Nancy in his leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Another popular, but false, myth claims his mother, Beverly, spilled his ashes at Heathrow Airport. Semi-reliable sources claim his ashes never left America, with his mother reportedly taking them to King David Cemetery in Philadelphia, where Nancy was buried, hopping a fence to dump them on Nancy's grave against her parents' wishes. "Sid Vicious, ex of the sex pistols, died of a heroin overdose in his sleep in the early morning hours of February 2nd, 1979."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Sid Vicious's Inability to Play Bass
xref.body: Glenn Matlock was fired from the Sex Pistols in 1977 for allegedly liking The Beatles, which was considered a "crime" within the band. His replacement was a fan named Sid Vicious, who was chosen for his cool look and punk-rock attitude, even though he could not play the bass. During the band's last tour in America in late 1977 and their final original show at the Winterland Ballroom in San Francisco on January 14, 1978, Sid appeared on stage but did not play a note; roadies were instructed to unplug him, and another musician played his bass parts behind the amplifiers.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Signing with Atlantic Records
xref.body: The band ultimately signed an 80/20 split deal with Atlantic Records for the world and America, while Warner Canada retained rights for Canada. This decision was influenced by the legendary status of Atlantic, known for artists like Led Zeppelin. They even met Ahmet Ertegun, one of Atlantic's co-founders, in his office on the day of signing, where they saw Jimmy Page's bow from "The Song Remains the Same" on the wall. "And so we decided to go with Atlantic records, which was the originally in our guys that we had seen that came up."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The Talking Heads were among the inaugural bands branded as "New Wave" by Sire Records, contributing to the establishment of the term in North America by the end of 1977. "The Talking Hits, one of the first bands branded by Sire Records as New Wave."

xref.title: Small Town Perspective on Life and Music
xref.body: Trent Reznor articulated his experience growing up in small-town America, noting a limited scope of travel and the uniformity of amenities like Kmarts and movie theaters showing the same five Sylvester Stallone films. He felt playing music wasn't considered "cool" and that being in the band rather than the football team made you a "leper." "My scope of travel was maybe a half hour radius, and every town had the same Kmart and synoplex, all playing the same five movies, all Sylvester Stallone. It's hard for people who grow up in cities to understand that, to have an endless cornfield in your backyard. But that's what a lot of America is. It's not dodging gunfire from gangs. It wasn't cool to play music where I was, and I got a pretty bad education because I had a bad attitude. If I wanted to get good grades, I could. Stuff I'd like to know now, at the time, I thought was irrelevant. Typical teenage stupidity. I hated school. The fact that it revolved around something you didn't have access to. If you weren't on the football team and you were in the band, you were a leper. When people say those are the best years of our lives, I want to scream. But my parents allowed me to do things that my friends weren't allowed to do."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.body: The New York Dolls were notable for their "Spandex and makeup wearing" style, emblematic of the glitter rock movement that found a home in America. "the Spandex and makeup wearing New York dolls."

xref.body: Thanks to endless touring and strong support from SST Records, Husker Dew's influence spread throughout North America. They became one of the first bands to rise through the indie ranks and sign with a major label, yet they maintained their uncompromising do-it-yourself ethic until the very end. "Thanks to endless touring and strong support from SST, Husker Dew was able to spread their influence to all corners of North America."

xref.title: Subpop's Hype Strategy
xref.body: Subpop owners Jonathan Poe and Bruce Pabbitt aimed to make Nirvana a sensation in the UK first, mirroring Jimi Hendrix's path to success, before breaking them in America. They flew a Melody Maker writer to Seattle to generate hype for Nirvana and other acts. "Why couldn't they do the same thing with bands like Nirvana?"

xref.title: Success Through Music Videos
xref.body: The gamble on high-quality, exotic music videos paid off immensely for Duran Duran. Their visual content, coupled with their New Wave sound, propelled them to massive record sales, contributing to the explosion of New Wave in North America. "The gamble worked, and they sold a gazillion records."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Success in Japan vs. North America
xref.body: During their four years together (1975-1979), The Runaways struggled to establish a significant career in North America. However, they were a sensation in Japan, where they achieved considerable commercial success and even recorded a live album in 1977. "But in Japan, it's another story. They were quite the sensation."

xref.title: The Toasters – Founded by British Expat Rob Hingley in New York; Most Important American Ska Band of the 1980s; Founded Moon Ska Records
xref.body: The Toasters were the most important American ska band of the 1980s. Founder Rob Hingley was a Brit who moved to New York only to find almost no one knew about the British ska scene, so he formed a band based on Two-Tone traditions. Beyond touring and recording, Hingley also established Moon Ska Records, which eventually became the largest and most important independent ska label in America, distributing dozens of bands across the continent. Moon Ska Records had a business until 2000, though some European operations survived. "Out of all the Skah bands of the early and middle 80s, no American group did more to popularize this sound in the US than the Toasters."

xref.title: Touring Challenges
xref.body: The band experienced significant disparity in audience numbers during their early tours. For example, they played a successful show at the Croatian Cultural Center in Vancouver to a thousand people with Billy Talent, only to cross the border into Bellingham, Washington, and play for only the bar staff, with Dallas Green not even performing due to voice issues. Later, attempts to "hammer it" in America during the "Old Crows" era, including a "disastrous" Warped Tour and long unfulfilling American tours where only 40-60% of shows were good, became mentally exhausting. "We played for the bar staff. I don't even think I played the show. You didn't. I didn't. I took a T-shirt. Because your voice was bothering you."

xref.body: A species of tree frog, *Dendro's Sophos Sting-I*, was named after Sting when it was discovered in 1994. This naming honors Sting's significant efforts in conservation, specifically his work to protect the rainforests of South America. "This is a species of tree frog that was named after Sting when it was discovered in 1994. Why would they name it that? xref.body: Jimi Hendrix, originally from Seattle, became a sensation in the UK in the 1960s long before breaking out in America. This historical precedent inspired Subpop record label owners to try a similar strategy for their grunge bands like Nirvana. "See Jimmy was from Seattle too, but back in the 1960s, he became a sensation in the UK long before he broke an America."

xref.title: UK Debut and Impact
xref.body: On July 4th, 1976, while America celebrated its Bicentennial, the Ramones played second on the bill at the Roundhouse in North London. This event is widely credited with doing "more to kick start British punk than anything else that had happened up until that point." "That event did more to kick start British punk than anything else that had happened up until that point."

xref.title: UK Success vs. North American Status
xref.body: The Lightning Seeds are not considered one-hit wonders in the UK, where they had a series of hit singles, including a number one in 1998 (an official World Cup song). However, in North America, only "Pure" achieved lasting recognition. "For North America, though, only two songs cut through, but only one really seems to have hung on over the decades."

xref.title: US Market Struggles (1990s onward)
xref.body: The Tragically Hip never achieved major stardom in the American market, a phenomenon that has become an area of study. While they have pockets of support, their timing often did not align with prevailing American rock trends. For instance, in the 1990s, American rock was dominated by grunge, then hip hop, and later indie rock (like The Strokes or The White Stripes), none of which perfectly matched the Hip's style. "Why has the tragically hip never been able to break through in the States? While this isn't entirely true, the hip do have pockets of support in America. But unlike Brian Adams or Lannis Morsehsett or Nickelback, it just seems that their timing was off. Their music was great, but whenever they were hot, American rock and roll attitudes were somewhere else. In the 90s, it was grunge, and the hip are not grunge. Then came hip hop. Hip didn't belong there. Then it was Indy Rock and the flavor of the strokes, so the white stripes and the hip didn't really fit in there either."

xref.title: US Tour with The Trews
xref.body: Ace Frehley toured the United States with The Trews as his opening act for a six-week trek, performing in House of Blues venues across the country. The audiences for these shows were predominantly "die-hard Kiss fans" who were not necessarily open to new music. "We ended up doing like six week trek, opening for Ace Freyly at House of Blues all over America."

xref.title: Uncredited Backing Band for Elvis Costello
xref.body: Clover was an American band that found itself broke while touring the UK. They were hired by Jake Riviera of Stiff Records to back Elvis Costello on his debut album, My Aim Is True, recording through late 1976 and early 1977 in a tiny studio in Islington, London. Due to contractual issues (another British band was already named Clover), they used the pseudonym The Sham Rocks and were never credited on the original album release. "So Riviera found a band called Clover, who had come over from America, and were pretty much broke as they tried to or the UK."

xref.title: Unexpected Early International Success
xref.body: Contrary to their initial expectations, Kings of Leon's first significant success came not in North America, but predominantly in the UK and Europe, which was unusual for a band originating from Tennessee. The band had believed their sound would first resonate in the American South, only to find the South was "one of the last places to get it," while audiences in places like Ireland were already singing their songs. "Your first seat of success, it wasn't in America, it wasn't in North America, it was in the UK and Europe, which is unexpected for a band from Tennessee."

xref.title: Unique Rock and Roll Philosophy
xref.body: In the early 1990s, the Manics distinguished themselves by professing to have more in common with American hard rock bands like Guns N' Roses and Motley Crue than with bands from Manchester or the emerging Britpop scene. They openly bragged about wanting to sell millions of records, a desire uncommon among indie bands of that era, and readily signed with a major label. "The Manics were different for the early 1990s. They professed to have more in common with guns and roses in Motley Crew than anything from Manchester or early Britpop, saying that real rock and roll came from America."

xref.body: Despite not fitting the prevalent guitar-heavy alt-rock sound in North America or the Britpop style in the UK, The Cranberries were signed in 1992 during a period of high demand for alternative bands, and successfully integrated into the growing alt-rock scene. "And even though the cranberries didn't fit with the usual guitar-heavy stuff that was happening in North America, or even the pre-briot pop stuff that was happening in the UK, they nevertheless became part of the growing alt-roxene."
